# email_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/email_address/

## Expand description

A Rust crate providing an implementation of an RFC-compliant `EmailAddress` newtype.

Primarily for validation, the `EmailAddress` type is constructed with `FromStr::from_str` which will raise any
parsing errors. Prior to constructions the functions `is_valid`, `is_valid_local_part`, and `is_valid_domain` may
also be used to test for validity without constructing an instance. This supports all of the RFC ASCII and UTF-8
character set rules, quoted and unquoted local parts but does not yet support all of the productions required for SMTP
headers; folding whitespace, comments, etc.

```
"Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>"
                 ^------------------^ email()
                            ^-------^ domain()
                 ^--------^ local_part()
 ^------------^ display_part()
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following shoes the basic `is_valid` and `from_str` functions.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
assert!(EmailAddress::is_valid("user.name+tag+sorting@example.com"));
assert_eq!(
    EmailAddress::from_str("Abc.example.com"),
    Error::MissingSeparator.into()
);
```
The following shows the three format functions used to output an email address.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
let email = EmailAddress::from_str("johnstonsk@gmail.com").unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    email.to_string(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    String::from(email.clone()),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.as_ref(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com"
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_uri(),
    "mailto:johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_display("Simon Johnston"),
    "Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>".to_string()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#specifications)Specifications

- RFC 1123: *Requirements for Internet Hosts – Application and Support*
- RFC 3629: *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*
- RFC 3696: *Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names*
- RFC 4291 *IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture*
- RFC 5234: *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*
- RFC 5321: *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*
- RFC 5322: *Internet Message Format*
- RFC 5890: *Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework*
- RFC 6531: *SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email*
- RFC 6532: *Internationalized Email Headers*

From RFC 5322: §3.2.1. [Quoted characters](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.1):

`quoted-pair     =   ("\" (VCHAR / WSP)) / obs-qp`From RFC 5322: §3.2.2. [Folding White Space and Comments](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.2):

```
FWS             =   ([*WSP CRLF] 1*WSP) /  obs-FWS
                                       ; Folding white space
ctext           =   %d33-39 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d42-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "(", ")", or "\"
                    obs-ctext
ccontent        =   ctext / quoted-pair / comment
comment         =   "(" *([FWS] ccontent) [FWS] ")"
CFWS            =   (1*([FWS] comment) [FWS]) / FWS
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.3. [Atom](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.3):

```
atext           =   ALPHA / DIGIT /    ; Printable US-ASCII
                    "!" / "#" /        ;  characters not including
                    "$" / "%" /        ;  specials.  Used for atoms.
                    "&" / "'" /
                    "*" / "+" /
                    "-" / "/" /
                    "=" / "?" /
                    "^" / "_" /
                    "`" / "{" /
                    "|" / "}" /
                    "~"
atom            =   [CFWS] 1*atext [CFWS]
dot-atom-text   =   1*atext *("." 1*atext)
dot-atom        =   [CFWS] dot-atom-text [CFWS]
specials        =   "(" / ")" /        ; Special characters that do
                    "<" / ">" /        ;  not appear in atext
                    "[" / "]" /
                    ":" / ";" /
                    "@" / "\" /
                    "," / "." /
                    DQUOTE
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.4. [Quoted Strings](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.4):

```
qtext           =   %d33 /             ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d35-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "\" or the quote character
                    obs-qtext
qcontent        =   qtext / quoted-pair
quoted-string   =   [CFWS]
                    DQUOTE *([FWS] qcontent) [FWS] DQUOTE
                    [CFWS]
```
From RFC 5322, §3.4.1. [Addr-Spec Specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.4.1):

```
addr-spec       =   local-part "@" domain
local-part      =   dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part
domain          =   dot-atom / domain-literal / obs-domain
domain-literal  =   [CFWS] "[" *([FWS] dtext) [FWS] "]" [CFWS]
dtext           =   %d33-90 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d94-126 /         ;  characters not including
                    obs-dtext          ;  "[", "]", or "\"
```
RFC 3696, §3. [Restrictions on email addresses](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3696#section-3)
describes in detail the quoting of characters in an address.

[§](https://docs.rs#unicode)Unicode

RFC 6531, §3.3. [Extended Mailbox Address Syntax](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6531#section-3.3)
extends the rules above for non-ASCII character sets.

```
sub-domain   =/  U-label
    ; extend the definition of sub-domain in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the implicit definition of atext in
    ; RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2, which ultimately points to
    ; the actual definition in RFC 5322, Section 3.2.3
qtextSMTP  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of qtextSMTP in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
esmtp-value  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of esmtp-value in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
```
A “U-label” is an IDNA-valid string of Unicode characters, in Normalization Form C (NFC) and including at least one non-ASCII character, expressed in a standard Unicode Encoding Form (such as UTF-8). It is also subject to the constraints about permitted characters that are specified in Section 4.2 of the Protocol document and the rules in the Sections 2 and 3 of the Tables document, the Bidi constraints in that document if it contains any character from scripts that are written right to left, and the symmetry constraint described immediately below. Conversions between U-labels and A-labels are performed according to the “Punycode” specification RFC3492, adding or removing the ACE prefix as needed.

RFC 6532: §3.1 [UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.1),
and §3.2 [Syntax Extensions to RFC 5322](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.2) extend
the syntax above with:

```
UTF8-non-ascii  =   UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
...
VCHAR   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
ctext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
qtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
text    =/  UTF8-non-ascii
              ; note that this upgrades the body to UTF-8
dtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
```
These in turn refer to RFC 6529 §4. [Syntax of UTF-8 Byte Sequences](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3629#section-4):

A UTF-8 string is a sequence of octets representing a sequence of UCS characters. An octet sequence is valid UTF-8 only if it matches the following syntax, which is derived from the rules for encoding UTF-8 and is expressed in the ABNF of [RFC2234].

```
   UTF8-octets = *( UTF8-char )
   UTF8-char   = UTF8-1 / UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
   UTF8-1      = %x00-7F
   UTF8-2      = %xC2-DF UTF8-tail
   UTF8-3      = %xE0 %xA0-BF UTF8-tail / %xE1-EC 2( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xED %x80-9F UTF8-tail / %xEE-EF 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-4      = %xF0 %x90-BF 2( UTF8-tail ) / %xF1-F3 3( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xF4 %x80-8F 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-tail   = %x80-BF
```
Comments in addresses are discussed in RFC 5322 Appendix A.5. [White Space, Comments, and Other
Oddities](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#appendix-A.5).

An informal description can be found on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_address).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Email](https://docs.rs/struct.EmailAddress.html)- Address
- Type representing a single email address. This is basically a wrapper around a String, the
email address is parsed for correctness with `FromStr::from_str`, which is the only want to create an instance. The various components of the email*are not*parsed out to be accessible independently.
- [Options](https://docs.rs/struct.Options.html)
- Struct of options that can be configured when parsing with `parse_with_options`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error type used when parsing an address.

# email_address 0.2.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/email_address/latest

# Crate email_address

A Rust crate providing an implementation of an RFC-compliant `EmailAddress` newtype.

Primarily for validation, the `EmailAddress` type is constructed with
`FromStr::from_str` which will raise any parsing errors. Prior to constructions
the functions `is_valid`, `is_valid_local_part`, and `is_valid_domain` may also be
used to test for validity without constructing an instance.

## Status

Currently, it supports all the RFC ASCII and UTF-8 character set rules as well as quoted and unquoted local parts but does not yet support all the productions required for SMTP headers; folding whitespace, comments, etc.

## Example

```
use *;
assert!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Specifications

- RFC 1123: *Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support*
- RFC 3629: *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*
- RFC 3696: *Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names*
- RFC 4291 *IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture*
- RFC 5234: *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*
- RFC 5321: *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*
- RFC 5322: *Internet Message Format*
- RFC 5890: *Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework*
- RFC 6531: *SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email*
- RFC 6532: *Internationalized Email Headers*

- Feature: Pull Request #18 -- Error with `SubDomainEmpty`when empty instead of`InvalidCharacter`.
- Feature: Pull Request #19 -- Allow configuring minimum number of subdomains.
- Feature: Pull Request #20 -- Add option to disallow domain literals.
- Feature: Pull Request #22 -- Handle a single qoute in local part of email

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

# serde_assert - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_assert/^0.8.0/

## Expand description

Testing library for `serde`[ Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html) and

[implementations.](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`This library provides a [ Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html) and

[to be used in writing unit tests to assert the behavior of manual](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)

`Deserializer`[and](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html)

`Serialize`[implementations, respectively. The implementation behavior can be verified by using a sequence of](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html)

`Deserialize`[s representing an arbitrary serialized state.](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)

`Token`[§](https://docs.rs#testing-serialization)Testing Serialization

The [ Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html) returns a sequence of

[s representing the serialization of a value. The returned](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)

`Token``Token`s can be checked to be equal to an expected value. Since
[returns a](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html#tymethod.serialize)

`Serialize::serialize()``Result<Tokens, Error>`, it is recommended to use the
[crate to check that the returned value is both](https://docs.rs/claims/)

`claims``Ok` and equal to the expected
sequence of `Token`s.```
use claims::assert_ok_eq;
use serde::Serialize;
use serde_assert::{
    Serializer,
    Token,
};
let serializer = Serializer::builder().build();
assert_ok_eq!(true.serialize(&serializer), [Token::Bool(true)]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-ordering)Arbitrary Ordering

In cases where the ordering of [ Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)s does not matter, such as when serializing a

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)

`HashSet`[can be used to specify that tokens can be in an arbitrary order.](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html#variant.Unordered)

`Token::Unordered````
use claims::assert_ok_eq;
use serde::Serialize;
use serde_assert::{
    Serializer,
    Token,
};
use std::collections::HashSet;
let serializer = Serializer::builder().build();
let mut set = HashSet::<u32>::new();
set.insert(1);
set.insert(2);
set.insert(3);
assert_ok_eq!(
    set.serialize(&serializer),
    [
        Token::Seq { len: Some(3) },
        Token::Unordered(&[&[Token::U32(1)], &[Token::U32(2)], &[Token::U32(3)],]),
        Token::SeqEnd
    ]
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing-deserialization)Testing Deserialization

A [ Deserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html) is constructed by providing a sequence of

[s to be deserialized into a value. During testing, the](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)

`Token`[crate can be used to assert that deserialization succeeds and returns the expected value.](https://docs.rs/claims/)

`claims````
use claims::assert_ok_eq;
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_assert::{
    Deserializer,
    Token,
};
let mut deserializer = Deserializer::builder([Token::Bool(true)]).build();
assert_ok_eq!(bool::deserialize(&mut deserializer), true);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing-roundtrip)Testing Roundtrip

To assert that a value remains the same when serialized and then deserialized again, the output
of the [ Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html) can be used as input to the

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)

`Deserializer````
use claims::{
    assert_ok,
    assert_ok_eq,
};
use serde::{
    Deserialize,
    Serialize,
};
use serde_assert::{
    Deserializer,
    Serializer,
};
let value = true;
let serializer = Serializer::builder().build();
let mut deserializer = Deserializer::builder(assert_ok!(value.serialize(&serializer))).build();
assert_ok_eq!(bool::deserialize(&mut deserializer), value);
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)

- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Testing serialization implementations.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing a serialized object.

- Deserializer for testing `Deserialize`

# email_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/email_address/latest/target-redirect/email_address/

## Expand description

A Rust crate providing an implementation of an RFC-compliant `EmailAddress` newtype.

Primarily for validation, the `EmailAddress` type is constructed with `FromStr::from_str` which will raise any
parsing errors. Prior to constructions the functions `is_valid`, `is_valid_local_part`, and `is_valid_domain` may
also be used to test for validity without constructing an instance. This supports all of the RFC ASCII and UTF-8
character set rules, quoted and unquoted local parts but does not yet support all of the productions required for SMTP
headers; folding whitespace, comments, etc.

```
"Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>"
                 ^------------------^ email()
                            ^-------^ domain()
                 ^--------^ local_part()
 ^------------^ display_part()
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following shoes the basic `is_valid` and `from_str` functions.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
assert!(EmailAddress::is_valid("user.name+tag+sorting@example.com"));
assert_eq!(
    EmailAddress::from_str("Abc.example.com"),
    Error::MissingSeparator.into()
);
```
The following shows the three format functions used to output an email address.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
let email = EmailAddress::from_str("johnstonsk@gmail.com").unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    email.to_string(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    String::from(email.clone()),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.as_ref(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com"
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_uri(),
    "mailto:johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_display("Simon Johnston"),
    "Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>".to_string()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#specifications)Specifications

- RFC 1123: *Requirements for Internet Hosts – Application and Support*
- RFC 3629: *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*
- RFC 3696: *Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names*
- RFC 4291 *IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture*
- RFC 5234: *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*
- RFC 5321: *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*
- RFC 5322: *Internet Message Format*
- RFC 5890: *Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework*
- RFC 6531: *SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email*
- RFC 6532: *Internationalized Email Headers*

From RFC 5322: §3.2.1. [Quoted characters](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.1):

`quoted-pair     =   ("\" (VCHAR / WSP)) / obs-qp`From RFC 5322: §3.2.2. [Folding White Space and Comments](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.2):

```
FWS             =   ([*WSP CRLF] 1*WSP) /  obs-FWS
                                       ; Folding white space
ctext           =   %d33-39 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d42-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "(", ")", or "\"
                    obs-ctext
ccontent        =   ctext / quoted-pair / comment
comment         =   "(" *([FWS] ccontent) [FWS] ")"
CFWS            =   (1*([FWS] comment) [FWS]) / FWS
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.3. [Atom](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.3):

```
atext           =   ALPHA / DIGIT /    ; Printable US-ASCII
                    "!" / "#" /        ;  characters not including
                    "$" / "%" /        ;  specials.  Used for atoms.
                    "&" / "'" /
                    "*" / "+" /
                    "-" / "/" /
                    "=" / "?" /
                    "^" / "_" /
                    "`" / "{" /
                    "|" / "}" /
                    "~"
atom            =   [CFWS] 1*atext [CFWS]
dot-atom-text   =   1*atext *("." 1*atext)
dot-atom        =   [CFWS] dot-atom-text [CFWS]
specials        =   "(" / ")" /        ; Special characters that do
                    "<" / ">" /        ;  not appear in atext
                    "[" / "]" /
                    ":" / ";" /
                    "@" / "\" /
                    "," / "." /
                    DQUOTE
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.4. [Quoted Strings](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.4):

```
qtext           =   %d33 /             ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d35-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "\" or the quote character
                    obs-qtext
qcontent        =   qtext / quoted-pair
quoted-string   =   [CFWS]
                    DQUOTE *([FWS] qcontent) [FWS] DQUOTE
                    [CFWS]
```
From RFC 5322, §3.4.1. [Addr-Spec Specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.4.1):

```
addr-spec       =   local-part "@" domain
local-part      =   dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part
domain          =   dot-atom / domain-literal / obs-domain
domain-literal  =   [CFWS] "[" *([FWS] dtext) [FWS] "]" [CFWS]
dtext           =   %d33-90 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d94-126 /         ;  characters not including
                    obs-dtext          ;  "[", "]", or "\"
```
RFC 3696, §3. [Restrictions on email addresses](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3696#section-3)
describes in detail the quoting of characters in an address.

[§](https://docs.rs#unicode)Unicode

RFC 6531, §3.3. [Extended Mailbox Address Syntax](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6531#section-3.3)
extends the rules above for non-ASCII character sets.

```
sub-domain   =/  U-label
    ; extend the definition of sub-domain in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the implicit definition of atext in
    ; RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2, which ultimately points to
    ; the actual definition in RFC 5322, Section 3.2.3
qtextSMTP  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of qtextSMTP in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
esmtp-value  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of esmtp-value in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
```
A “U-label” is an IDNA-valid string of Unicode characters, in Normalization Form C (NFC) and including at least one non-ASCII character, expressed in a standard Unicode Encoding Form (such as UTF-8). It is also subject to the constraints about permitted characters that are specified in Section 4.2 of the Protocol document and the rules in the Sections 2 and 3 of the Tables document, the Bidi constraints in that document if it contains any character from scripts that are written right to left, and the symmetry constraint described immediately below. Conversions between U-labels and A-labels are performed according to the “Punycode” specification RFC3492, adding or removing the ACE prefix as needed.

RFC 6532: §3.1 [UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.1),
and §3.2 [Syntax Extensions to RFC 5322](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.2) extend
the syntax above with:

```
UTF8-non-ascii  =   UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
...
VCHAR   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
ctext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
qtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
text    =/  UTF8-non-ascii
              ; note that this upgrades the body to UTF-8
dtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
```
These in turn refer to RFC 6529 §4. [Syntax of UTF-8 Byte Sequences](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3629#section-4):

A UTF-8 string is a sequence of octets representing a sequence of UCS characters. An octet sequence is valid UTF-8 only if it matches the following syntax, which is derived from the rules for encoding UTF-8 and is expressed in the ABNF of [RFC2234].

```
   UTF8-octets = *( UTF8-char )
   UTF8-char   = UTF8-1 / UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
   UTF8-1      = %x00-7F
   UTF8-2      = %xC2-DF UTF8-tail
   UTF8-3      = %xE0 %xA0-BF UTF8-tail / %xE1-EC 2( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xED %x80-9F UTF8-tail / %xEE-EF 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-4      = %xF0 %x90-BF 2( UTF8-tail ) / %xF1-F3 3( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xF4 %x80-8F 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-tail   = %x80-BF
```
Comments in addresses are discussed in RFC 5322 Appendix A.5. [White Space, Comments, and Other
Oddities](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#appendix-A.5).

An informal description can be found on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_address).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rship_shared_schemas - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rship-shared-schemas/4.0.0-canary.63/rship_shared_schemas/

## Expand description

Shared schema registry.

Hosts the `WellKnownSchema` enum (a closed set of schemas every SDK knows
about) and the `SchemaRef` reference type used by `Action`, `Emitter`, and
comp-engine entities. Generated to every SDK via typegen so misspelled or
invented schema ids are unrepresentable at compile time.

See `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-30-comp-engine-design.md`
§ “Shared-Schemas Registry”.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use registry::`- [GetAllSchemas](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetAllSchemas.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetAllSchemasOutput](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetAllSchemasOutput.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetSchemaByVariant](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetSchemaByVariant.html);
- `pub use registry::`- [GetSchemaByVariantOutput](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.GetSchemaByVariantOutput.html);
- `pub use schema_ref::`- [SchemaRef](https://docs.rs/schema_ref/enum.SchemaRef.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [SchemaEntry](https://docs.rs/well_known/struct.SchemaEntry.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [SchemaSemantic](https://docs.rs/well_known/enum.SchemaSemantic.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [WellKnownSchema](https://docs.rs/well_known/enum.WellKnownSchema.html);
- `pub use well_known::`- [schema_for](https://docs.rs/well_known/fn.schema_for.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [registry](https://docs.rs/registry/index.html)
- Server-side reports for inspecting the shared-schemas registry from the UI.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/schema_ref/index.html)- ref
- Typed schema-reference enum used by Action, Emitter, and downstream
entities. Prefer `SchemaRef::WellKnown(...)`at call sites; reach for`SchemaRef::Custom(...)`only when no well-known schema fits the value.
- [well_](https://docs.rs/well_known/index.html)- known
- Well-known schema enum — the closed set of schemas rship core knows about.
Every variant has exactly one registered body. Adding a variant requires
extending the exhaustive match in `schema_for`; missing a variant fails to compile.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [link](https://docs.rs/fn.link.html)
- Touch this from `typegen`and other binaries to force the linker to keep the`inventory::submit!`registrations alive.

# yoagent_state - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yoagent-state/0.4.0/yoagent_state/

## Expand description

Simple but effective state and lineage for long-running agents.

`yoagent-state` stores append-only events and derives a small semantic graph
for patches, evals, decisions, artifacts, and project references. Git and the
filesystem remain the source of truth for concrete project changes.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- In-process sink for callback-driven agents — the integration contract as a
typed interface. `YoAgentStateAdapter`routes the entity-creating callbacks (run start/finish, model/tool calls, tool failures) through the paired`record_*`helpers and records the non-entity-creating finish events (`model.finished`,`tool.finished`) raw, auto-chained and correlated to the open run — so a log emitted through the sink is GASP-conformant: runs open/close (with validation), tool and model calls become paired nodes chained to the run, and failures carry ids and pairs.

# email_address 0.2.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/email_address/0.2.9

# Crate email_address

A Rust crate providing an implementation of an RFC-compliant `EmailAddress` newtype.

Primarily for validation, the `EmailAddress` type is constructed with
`FromStr::from_str` which will raise any parsing errors. Prior to constructions
the functions `is_valid`, `is_valid_local_part`, and `is_valid_domain` may also be
used to test for validity without constructing an instance.

## Status

Currently, it supports all the RFC ASCII and UTF-8 character set rules as well as quoted and unquoted local parts but does not yet support all the productions required for SMTP headers; folding whitespace, comments, etc.

## Example

```
use *;
assert!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Specifications

- RFC 1123: *Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support*
- RFC 3629: *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*
- RFC 3696: *Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names*
- RFC 4291 *IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture*
- RFC 5234: *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*
- RFC 5321: *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*
- RFC 5322: *Internet Message Format*
- RFC 5890: *Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework*
- RFC 6531: *SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email*
- RFC 6532: *Internationalized Email Headers*

## Changes

# email_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/email_address/0.2.9/target-redirect/email_address/

## Expand description

A Rust crate providing an implementation of an RFC-compliant `EmailAddress` newtype.

Primarily for validation, the `EmailAddress` type is constructed with `FromStr::from_str` which will raise any
parsing errors. Prior to constructions the functions `is_valid`, `is_valid_local_part`, and `is_valid_domain` may
also be used to test for validity without constructing an instance. This supports all of the RFC ASCII and UTF-8
character set rules, quoted and unquoted local parts but does not yet support all of the productions required for SMTP
headers; folding whitespace, comments, etc.

```
"Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>"
                 ^------------------^ email()
                            ^-------^ domain()
                 ^--------^ local_part()
 ^------------^ display_part()
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following shoes the basic `is_valid` and `from_str` functions.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
assert!(EmailAddress::is_valid("user.name+tag+sorting@example.com"));
assert_eq!(
    EmailAddress::from_str("Abc.example.com"),
    Error::MissingSeparator.into()
);
```
The following shows the three format functions used to output an email address.

```
use email_address::*;
use std::str::FromStr;
let email = EmailAddress::from_str("johnstonsk@gmail.com").unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    email.to_string(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    String::from(email.clone()),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.as_ref(),
    "johnstonsk@gmail.com"
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_uri(),
    "mailto:johnstonsk@gmail.com".to_string()
);
assert_eq!(
    email.to_display("Simon Johnston"),
    "Simon Johnston <johnstonsk@gmail.com>".to_string()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#specifications)Specifications

- RFC 1123: *Requirements for Internet Hosts – Application and Support*
- RFC 3629: *UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646*
- RFC 3696: *Application Techniques for Checking and Transformation of Names*
- RFC 4291 *IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture*
- RFC 5234: *Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF*
- RFC 5321: *Simple Mail Transfer Protocol*
- RFC 5322: *Internet Message Format*
- RFC 5890: *Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA): Definitions and Document Framework*
- RFC 6531: *SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email*
- RFC 6532: *Internationalized Email Headers*

From RFC 5322: §3.2.1. [Quoted characters](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.1):

`quoted-pair     =   ("\" (VCHAR / WSP)) / obs-qp`From RFC 5322: §3.2.2. [Folding White Space and Comments](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.2):

```
FWS             =   ([*WSP CRLF] 1*WSP) /  obs-FWS
                                       ; Folding white space
ctext           =   %d33-39 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d42-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "(", ")", or "\"
                    obs-ctext
ccontent        =   ctext / quoted-pair / comment
comment         =   "(" *([FWS] ccontent) [FWS] ")"
CFWS            =   (1*([FWS] comment) [FWS]) / FWS
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.3. [Atom](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.3):

```
atext           =   ALPHA / DIGIT /    ; Printable US-ASCII
                    "!" / "#" /        ;  characters not including
                    "$" / "%" /        ;  specials.  Used for atoms.
                    "&" / "'" /
                    "*" / "+" /
                    "-" / "/" /
                    "=" / "?" /
                    "^" / "_" /
                    "`" / "{" /
                    "|" / "}" /
                    "~"
atom            =   [CFWS] 1*atext [CFWS]
dot-atom-text   =   1*atext *("." 1*atext)
dot-atom        =   [CFWS] dot-atom-text [CFWS]
specials        =   "(" / ")" /        ; Special characters that do
                    "<" / ">" /        ;  not appear in atext
                    "[" / "]" /
                    ":" / ";" /
                    "@" / "\" /
                    "," / "." /
                    DQUOTE
```
From RFC 5322: §3.2.4. [Quoted Strings](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.4):

```
qtext           =   %d33 /             ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d35-91 /          ;  characters not including
                    %d93-126 /         ;  "\" or the quote character
                    obs-qtext
qcontent        =   qtext / quoted-pair
quoted-string   =   [CFWS]
                    DQUOTE *([FWS] qcontent) [FWS] DQUOTE
                    [CFWS]
```
From RFC 5322, §3.4.1. [Addr-Spec Specification](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.4.1):

```
addr-spec       =   local-part "@" domain
local-part      =   dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part
domain          =   dot-atom / domain-literal / obs-domain
domain-literal  =   [CFWS] "[" *([FWS] dtext) [FWS] "]" [CFWS]
dtext           =   %d33-90 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
                    %d94-126 /         ;  characters not including
                    obs-dtext          ;  "[", "]", or "\"
```
RFC 3696, §3. [Restrictions on email addresses](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3696#section-3)
describes in detail the quoting of characters in an address.

[§](https://docs.rs#unicode)Unicode

RFC 6531, §3.3. [Extended Mailbox Address Syntax](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6531#section-3.3)
extends the rules above for non-ASCII character sets.

```
sub-domain   =/  U-label
    ; extend the definition of sub-domain in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the implicit definition of atext in
    ; RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2, which ultimately points to
    ; the actual definition in RFC 5322, Section 3.2.3
qtextSMTP  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of qtextSMTP in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
esmtp-value  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
    ; extend the definition of esmtp-value in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
```
A “U-label” is an IDNA-valid string of Unicode characters, in Normalization Form C (NFC) and including at least one non-ASCII character, expressed in a standard Unicode Encoding Form (such as UTF-8). It is also subject to the constraints about permitted characters that are specified in Section 4.2 of the Protocol document and the rules in the Sections 2 and 3 of the Tables document, the Bidi constraints in that document if it contains any character from scripts that are written right to left, and the symmetry constraint described immediately below. Conversions between U-labels and A-labels are performed according to the “Punycode” specification RFC3492, adding or removing the ACE prefix as needed.

RFC 6532: §3.1 [UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.1),
and §3.2 [Syntax Extensions to RFC 5322](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.2) extend
the syntax above with:

```
UTF8-non-ascii  =   UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
...
VCHAR   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
ctext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
qtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
text    =/  UTF8-non-ascii
              ; note that this upgrades the body to UTF-8
dtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
```
These in turn refer to RFC 6529 §4. [Syntax of UTF-8 Byte Sequences](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3629#section-4):

A UTF-8 string is a sequence of octets representing a sequence of UCS characters. An octet sequence is valid UTF-8 only if it matches the following syntax, which is derived from the rules for encoding UTF-8 and is expressed in the ABNF of [RFC2234].

```
   UTF8-octets = *( UTF8-char )
   UTF8-char   = UTF8-1 / UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
   UTF8-1      = %x00-7F
   UTF8-2      = %xC2-DF UTF8-tail
   UTF8-3      = %xE0 %xA0-BF UTF8-tail / %xE1-EC 2( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xED %x80-9F UTF8-tail / %xEE-EF 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-4      = %xF0 %x90-BF 2( UTF8-tail ) / %xF1-F3 3( UTF8-tail ) /
                 %xF4 %x80-8F 2( UTF8-tail )
   UTF8-tail   = %x80-BF
```
Comments in addresses are discussed in RFC 5322 Appendix A.5. [White Space, Comments, and Other
Oddities](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#appendix-A.5).

An informal description can be found on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_address).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Email](https://docs.rs/struct.EmailAddress.html)- Address
- Type representing a single email address. This is basically a wrapper around a String, the
email address is parsed for correctness with `FromStr::from_str`, which is the only want to create an instance. The various components of the email*are not*parsed out to be accessible independently.
- [Options](https://docs.rs/struct.Options.html)
- Struct of options that can be configured when parsing with `parse_with_options`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error type used when parsing an address.

[98](https://docs.rs#98)From RFC 5322: §3.2.2. [Folding White Space and Comments](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.2):
[99](https://docs.rs#99)
[100](https://docs.rs#100)```ebnf
[101](https://docs.rs#101)FWS             =   ([*WSP CRLF] 1*WSP) /  obs-FWS
[102](https://docs.rs#102)                                       ; Folding white space
[103](https://docs.rs#103)
[104](https://docs.rs#104)ctext           =   %d33-39 /          ; Printable US-ASCII
[105](https://docs.rs#105)                    %d42-91 /          ;  characters not including
[106](https://docs.rs#106)                    %d93-126 /         ;  "(", ")", or "\"
[107](https://docs.rs#107)                    obs-ctext
[108](https://docs.rs#108)
[109](https://docs.rs#109)ccontent        =   ctext / quoted-pair / comment
[110](https://docs.rs#110)
[111](https://docs.rs#111)comment         =   "(" *([FWS] ccontent) [FWS] ")"
[112](https://docs.rs#112)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)CFWS            =   (1*([FWS] comment) [FWS]) / FWS
[114](https://docs.rs#114)```

[116](https://docs.rs#116)From RFC 5322: §3.2.3. [Atom](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.3):
[117](https://docs.rs#117)
[118](https://docs.rs#118)```ebnf
[119](https://docs.rs#119)atext           =   ALPHA / DIGIT /    ; Printable US-ASCII
[120](https://docs.rs#120)                    "!" / "#" /        ;  characters not including
[121](https://docs.rs#121)                    "$" / "%" /        ;  specials.  Used for atoms.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)                    "&" / "'" /
[123](https://docs.rs#123)                    "*" / "+" /
[124](https://docs.rs#124)                    "-" / "/" /
[125](https://docs.rs#125)                    "=" / "?" /
[126](https://docs.rs#126)                    "^" / "_" /
[127](https://docs.rs#127)                    "`" / "{" /
[128](https://docs.rs#128)                    "|" / "}" /
[129](https://docs.rs#129)                    "~"
[130](https://docs.rs#130)
[131](https://docs.rs#131)atom            =   [CFWS] 1*atext [CFWS]
[132](https://docs.rs#132)
[133](https://docs.rs#133)dot-atom-text   =   1*atext *("." 1*atext)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)
[135](https://docs.rs#135)dot-atom        =   [CFWS] dot-atom-text [CFWS]
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)specials        =   "(" / ")" /        ; Special characters that do
[138](https://docs.rs#138)                    "<" / ">" /        ;  not appear in atext
[139](https://docs.rs#139)                    "[" / "]" /
[140](https://docs.rs#140)                    ":" / ";" /
[141](https://docs.rs#141)                    "@" / "\" /
[142](https://docs.rs#142)                    "," / "." /
[143](https://docs.rs#143)                    DQUOTE
[144](https://docs.rs#144)```
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)From RFC 5322: §3.2.4. [Quoted Strings](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#section-3.2.4):

[149](https://docs.rs#149)qtext           =   %d33 /             ; Printable US-ASCII

[179](https://docs.rs#179)
[180](https://docs.rs#180)## Unicode
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)RFC 6531, §3.3. [Extended Mailbox Address Syntax](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6531#section-3.3)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)extends the rules above for non-ASCII character sets.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)```ebnf
[186](https://docs.rs#186)sub-domain   =/  U-label
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    ; extend the definition of sub-domain in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    ; extend the implicit definition of atext in
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    ; RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2, which ultimately points to
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ; the actual definition in RFC 5322, Section 3.2.3
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)qtextSMTP  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    ; extend the definition of qtextSMTP in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
[196](https://docs.rs#196)
[197](https://docs.rs#197)esmtp-value  =/ UTF8-non-ascii
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    ; extend the definition of esmtp-value in RFC 5321, Section 4.1.2
[199](https://docs.rs#199)```
[200](https://docs.rs#200)
[201](https://docs.rs#201)A "U-label" is an IDNA-valid string of Unicode characters, in Normalization Form C (NFC) and
[202](https://docs.rs#202)including at least one non-ASCII character, expressed in a standard Unicode Encoding Form (such as
[203](https://docs.rs#203)UTF-8). It is also subject to the constraints about permitted characters that are specified in
[204](https://docs.rs#204)Section 4.2 of the Protocol document and the rules in the Sections 2 and 3 of the Tables document,
[205](https://docs.rs#205)the Bidi constraints in that document if it contains any character from scripts that are written
[206](https://docs.rs#206)right to left, and the symmetry constraint described immediately below. Conversions between U-labels
[207](https://docs.rs#207)and A-labels are performed according to the "Punycode" specification RFC3492, adding or removing
[208](https://docs.rs#208)the ACE prefix as needed.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)RFC 6532: §3.1 [UTF-8 Syntax and Normalization](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.1),
[211](https://docs.rs#211)and §3.2 [Syntax Extensions to RFC 5322](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6532#section-3.2) extend
[212](https://docs.rs#212)the syntax above with:
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)```ebnf
[215](https://docs.rs#215)UTF8-non-ascii  =   UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
[216](https://docs.rs#216)
[217](https://docs.rs#217)...
[218](https://docs.rs#218)
[219](https://docs.rs#219)VCHAR   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[220](https://docs.rs#220)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)ctext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)atext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)qtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[226](https://docs.rs#226)
[227](https://docs.rs#227)text    =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[228](https://docs.rs#228)              ; note that this upgrades the body to UTF-8
[229](https://docs.rs#229)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)dtext   =/  UTF8-non-ascii
[231](https://docs.rs#231)```
[232](https://docs.rs#232)
[233](https://docs.rs#233)These in turn refer to RFC 6529 §4. [Syntax of UTF-8 Byte Sequences](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3629#section-4):
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)> A UTF-8 string is a sequence of octets representing a sequence of UCS
[236](https://docs.rs#236)> characters.  An octet sequence is valid UTF-8 only if it matches the
[237](https://docs.rs#237)> following syntax, which is derived from the rules for encoding UTF-8
[238](https://docs.rs#238)> and is expressed in the ABNF of \[RFC2234\].
[239](https://docs.rs#239)
[240](https://docs.rs#240)```ebnf
[241](https://docs.rs#241)   UTF8-octets = *( UTF8-char )
[242](https://docs.rs#242)   UTF8-char   = UTF8-1 / UTF8-2 / UTF8-3 / UTF8-4
[243](https://docs.rs#243)   UTF8-1      = %x00-7F
[244](https://docs.rs#244)   UTF8-2      = %xC2-DF UTF8-tail
[245](https://docs.rs#245)   UTF8-3      = %xE0 %xA0-BF UTF8-tail / %xE1-EC 2( UTF8-tail ) /
[246](https://docs.rs#246)                 %xED %x80-9F UTF8-tail / %xEE-EF 2( UTF8-tail )
[247](https://docs.rs#247)   UTF8-4      = %xF0 %x90-BF 2( UTF8-tail ) / %xF1-F3 3( UTF8-tail ) /
[248](https://docs.rs#248)                 %xF4 %x80-8F 2( UTF8-tail )
[249](https://docs.rs#249)   UTF8-tail   = %x80-BF
[250](https://docs.rs#250)```
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)Comments in addresses are discussed in RFC 5322 Appendix A.5. [White Space, Comments, and Other
[253](https://docs.rs#253)Oddities](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5322#appendix-A.5).
[254](https://docs.rs#254)
[255](https://docs.rs#255)An informal description can be found on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email_address).

[308](https://docs.rs#308)///
[309](https://docs.rs#309)/// Error type used when parsing an address.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)///
[311](https://docs.rs#311)#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)pub enum Error {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// An invalid character was found in some component of the address.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    InvalidCharacter,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    /// The separator character between `local-part` and `domain` (character: '@') was missing.
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    MissingSeparator,
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// The `local-part` is an empty string.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    LocalPartEmpty,
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// The `local-part` is is too long.
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    LocalPartTooLong,
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// The `domain` is an empty string.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    DomainEmpty,
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    /// The `domain` is is too long.
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    DomainTooLong,
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// The `sub-domain` within the `domain` is empty.
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    SubDomainEmpty,
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    /// A `sub-domain` within the `domain` is is too long.
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    SubDomainTooLong,
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// Too few `sub-domain`s in `domain`.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    DomainTooFew,
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    /// Invalid placement of the domain separator (character: '.').
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    DomainInvalidSeparator,
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// The quotes (character: '"') around `local-part` are unbalanced.
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    UnbalancedQuotes,
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// A Comment within the either the `local-part`, or `domain`, was malformed.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    InvalidComment,
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// An IP address in a `domain-literal` was malformed.
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    InvalidIPAddress,
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// A `domain-literal` was supplied, but is unsupported by parser configuration.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    UnsupportedDomainLiteral,
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// Display name was supplied, but is unsupported by parser configuration.
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    UnsupportedDisplayName,
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// Display name was not supplied, but email starts with '<'.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    MissingDisplayName,
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// An email enclosed within <...> is missing the final '>'.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    MissingEndBracket,
[347](https://docs.rs#347)}
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)///
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// Struct of options that can be configured when parsing with `parse_with_options`.
[351](https://docs.rs#351)///
[352](https://docs.rs#352)#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone)]
[353](https://docs.rs#353)pub struct Options {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    ///
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// Sets the minimum number of domain segments that must exist to parse successfully.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    ///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    /// ```rust
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    /// use email_address::*;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    ///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    /// assert!(
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    ///         "simon@localhost",
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    ///         Options::default().with_no_minimum_sub_domains(),
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    ///     ).is_ok()
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// );
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// assert_eq!(
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///         "simon@localhost",
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    ///         Options::default().with_required_tld()
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    ///     ),
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    ///     Err(Error::DomainTooFew)
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    /// );
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// ```
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    ///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    pub minimum_sub_domains: usize,
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    ///
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    /// Specifies if domain literals are allowed. Defaults to `true`.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    ///
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// ```rust
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// use email_address::*;
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    ///
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// assert!(
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    ///         "email@[127.0.0.256]",
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///         Options::default().with_domain_literal()
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    ///     ).is_ok()
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// );
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    ///
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    /// assert_eq!(
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    ///         "email@[127.0.0.256]",
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///         Options::default().without_domain_literal()
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    ///     ),
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///     Err(Error::UnsupportedDomainLiteral),
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// );
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// ```
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    ///
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    pub allow_domain_literal: bool,
[400](https://docs.rs#400)
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    ///
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// Specified whether display text is allowed. Defaults to `true`. If you want strict
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// email-only checking setting this to `false` will remove support for the prefix string
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// and therefore the '<' and '>' brackets around the email part.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    ///
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// ```rust
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// use email_address::*;
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    ///
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// assert_eq!(
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    ///         "Simon <simon@example.com>",
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    ///         Options::default().without_display_text()
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///     ),
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    ///     Err(Error::UnsupportedDisplayName),
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// );
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    ///
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    /// assert_eq!(
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    ///     EmailAddress::parse_with_options(
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    ///         "<simon@example.com>",
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    ///         Options::default().without_display_text()
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    ///     ),
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///     Err(Error::InvalidCharacter),
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// );
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// ```
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    ///
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    pub allow_display_text: bool,
[427](https://docs.rs#427)}
[428](https://docs.rs#428)
[429](https://docs.rs#429)///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)/// Type representing a single email address. This is basically a wrapper around a String, the
[431](https://docs.rs#431)/// email address is parsed for correctness with `FromStr::from_str`, which is the only want to
[432](https://docs.rs#432)/// create an instance. The various components of the email _are not_ parsed out to be accessible
[433](https://docs.rs#433)/// independently.
[434](https://docs.rs#434)///
[435](https://docs.rs#435)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[436](https://docs.rs#436)pub struct EmailAddress(String);
[437](https://docs.rs#437)

[473](https://docs.rs#473)impl Display for Error {
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        match self {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            Error::InvalidCharacter => write!(f, "Invalid character."),
[477](https://docs.rs#477)            Error::LocalPartEmpty => write!(f, "Local part is empty."),
[478](https://docs.rs#478)            Error::LocalPartTooLong => write!(
[479](https://docs.rs#479)                f,
[480](https://docs.rs#480)                "Local part is too long. Length limit: {}",
[481](https://docs.rs#481)                LOCAL_PART_MAX_LENGTH
[482](https://docs.rs#482)            ),
[483](https://docs.rs#483)            Error::DomainEmpty => write!(f, "Domain is empty."),
[484](https://docs.rs#484)            Error::DomainTooLong => {
[485](https://docs.rs#485)                write!(f, "Domain is too long. Length limit: {}", DOMAIN_MAX_LENGTH)
[486](https://docs.rs#486)            }
[487](https://docs.rs#487)            Error::SubDomainEmpty => write!(f, "A sub-domain is empty."),
[488](https://docs.rs#488)            Error::SubDomainTooLong => write!(
[489](https://docs.rs#489)                f,
[490](https://docs.rs#490)                "A sub-domain is too long. Length limit: {}",
[491](https://docs.rs#491)                SUB_DOMAIN_MAX_LENGTH
[492](https://docs.rs#492)            ),
[493](https://docs.rs#493)            Error::MissingSeparator => write!(f, "Missing separator character '{}'.", AT),
[494](https://docs.rs#494)            Error::DomainTooFew => write!(f, "Too few parts in the domain"),
[495](https://docs.rs#495)            Error::DomainInvalidSeparator => {
[496](https://docs.rs#496)                write!(f, "Invalid placement of the domain separator '{:?}", DOT)
[497](https://docs.rs#497)            }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)            Error::InvalidIPAddress => write!(f, "Invalid IP Address specified for domain."),
[499](https://docs.rs#499)            Error::UnbalancedQuotes => write!(f, "Quotes around the local-part are unbalanced."),
[500](https://docs.rs#500)            Error::InvalidComment => write!(f, "A comment was badly formed."),
[501](https://docs.rs#501)            Error::UnsupportedDomainLiteral => write!(f, "Domain literals are not supported."),
[502](https://docs.rs#502)            Error::UnsupportedDisplayName => write!(f, "Display names are not supported."),
[503](https://docs.rs#503)            Error::MissingDisplayName => write!(
[504](https://docs.rs#504)                f,
[505](https://docs.rs#505)                "Display name was not supplied, but email starts with '<'."
[506](https://docs.rs#506)            ),
[507](https://docs.rs#507)            Error::MissingEndBracket => write!(f, "Terminating '>' is missing."),
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        }
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    }

[599](https://docs.rs#599)
[600](https://docs.rs#600)// From RFC 5321, section 2.4:
[601](https://docs.rs#601)//
[602](https://docs.rs#602)// The local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case sensitive. Therefore,
[603](https://docs.rs#603)// SMTP implementations MUST take care to preserve the case of mailbox
[604](https://docs.rs#604)// local-parts. In particular, for some hosts, the user "smith" is different
[605](https://docs.rs#605)// from the user "Smith". However, exploiting the case sensitivity of mailbox
[606](https://docs.rs#606)// local-parts impedes interoperability and is discouraged. Mailbox domains
[607](https://docs.rs#607)// follow normal DNS rules and are hence not case sensitive.
[608](https://docs.rs#608)//
[609](https://docs.rs#609)
[610](https://docs.rs#610)impl PartialEq for EmailAddress {
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    fn eq(&self, other: &Self) -> bool {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)        let (left, right) = split_at(&self.0).unwrap();
[613](https://docs.rs#613)        let (other_left, other_right) = split_at(&other.0).unwrap();
[614](https://docs.rs#614)        left.eq(other_left) && right.eq_ignore_ascii_case(other_right)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    }

[688](https://docs.rs#688)impl EmailAddress {
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    ///
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// Creates an `EmailAddress` without checking if the email is valid. Only
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    /// call this method if the address is known to be valid.
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    ///
[693](https://docs.rs#693)    /// ```
[694](https://docs.rs#694)    /// use std::str::FromStr;
[695](https://docs.rs#695)    /// use email_address::EmailAddress;
[696](https://docs.rs#696)    ///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    /// let unchecked = "john.doe@example.com";
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    /// let email = EmailAddress::from_str(unchecked).expect("email is not valid");
[699](https://docs.rs#699)    /// let valid_email = String::from(email);
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    /// let email = EmailAddress::new_unchecked(valid_email);
[701](https://docs.rs#701)    ///
[702](https://docs.rs#702)    /// assert_eq!("John Doe <john.doe@example.com>", email.to_display("John Doe"));
[703](https://docs.rs#703)    /// ```
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    pub fn new_unchecked<S>(address: S) -> Self

[706](https://docs.rs#706)        S: Into<String>,

[758](https://docs.rs#758)    ///
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    /// Return this email address formatted as a URI. This will also URI-encode the email

[770](https://docs.rs#770)    /// ```

[772](https://docs.rs#772)    pub fn to_uri(&self) -> String {

[774](https://docs.rs#774)        format!("{}{}", MAILTO_URI_PREFIX, encoded)
[775](https://docs.rs#775)    }

[795](https://docs.rs#795)
[796](https://docs.rs#796)    ///
[797](https://docs.rs#797)    /// Returns the local part of the email address. This is borrowed so that no additional
[798](https://docs.rs#798)    /// allocation is required.
[799](https://docs.rs#799)    ///
[800](https://docs.rs#800)    /// ```rust
[801](https://docs.rs#801)    /// use email_address::*;
[802](https://docs.rs#802)    /// use std::str::FromStr;
[803](https://docs.rs#803)    ///
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    /// assert_eq!(
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    ///     EmailAddress::from_str("name@example.org").unwrap().local_part(),
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    ///     String::from("name")
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    /// );
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    /// ```
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    ///

[884](https://docs.rs#884)fn encode(address: &str) -> String {
[885](https://docs.rs#885)    let mut result = String::new();
[886](https://docs.rs#886)    for c in address.chars() {
[887](https://docs.rs#887)        if is_uri_reserved(c) {

[891](https://docs.rs#891)        }

[896](https://docs.rs#896)fn is_uri_reserved(c: char) -> bool {

[898](https://docs.rs#898)    c == '!'
[899](https://docs.rs#899)        || c == '#'
[900](https://docs.rs#900)        || c == '$'
[901](https://docs.rs#901)        || c == '%'
[902](https://docs.rs#902)        || c == '&'
[903](https://docs.rs#903)        || c == '\''
[904](https://docs.rs#904)        || c == '('
[905](https://docs.rs#905)        || c == ')'
[906](https://docs.rs#906)        || c == '*'
[907](https://docs.rs#907)        || c == '+'
[908](https://docs.rs#908)        || c == ','
[909](https://docs.rs#909)        || c == '/'
[910](https://docs.rs#910)        || c == ':'
[911](https://docs.rs#911)        || c == ';'
[912](https://docs.rs#912)        || c == '='
[913](https://docs.rs#913)        || c == '?'

[918](https://docs.rs#918)fn parse_address(address: &str, options: Options) -> Result<EmailAddress, Error> {
[919](https://docs.rs#919)    //
[920](https://docs.rs#920)    // Deals with cases of '@' in `local-part`, if it is quoted they are legal, if
[921](https://docs.rs#921)    // not then they'll return an `InvalidCharacter` error later.
[922](https://docs.rs#922)    //
[923](https://docs.rs#923)    let (local_part, domain, display) = split_parts(address)?;
[924](https://docs.rs#924)    match (
[925](https://docs.rs#925)        display.is_empty(),
[926](https://docs.rs#926)        local_part.starts_with(DISPLAY_START),
[927](https://docs.rs#927)        options.allow_display_text,
[928](https://docs.rs#928)    ) {
[929](https://docs.rs#929)        (false, _, false) => Err(Error::UnsupportedDisplayName),
[930](https://docs.rs#930)        (true, true, true) => Err(Error::MissingDisplayName),
[931](https://docs.rs#931)        (true, true, false) => Err(Error::InvalidCharacter),
[932](https://docs.rs#932)        _ => {
[933](https://docs.rs#933)            parse_local_part(local_part, options)?;
[934](https://docs.rs#934)            parse_domain(domain, options)?;
[935](https://docs.rs#935)            Ok(EmailAddress(address.to_owned()))
[936](https://docs.rs#936)        }
[937](https://docs.rs#937)    }
[938](https://docs.rs#938)}

[940](https://docs.rs#940)fn split_parts(address: &str) -> Result<(&str, &str, &str), Error> {
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    let (display, email) = split_display_email(address)?;
[942](https://docs.rs#942)    let (local_part, domain) = split_at(email)?;
[943](https://docs.rs#943)    Ok((local_part, domain, display))
[944](https://docs.rs#944)}
[945](https://docs.rs#945)
[946](https://docs.rs#946)fn split_display_email(text: &str) -> Result<(&str, &str), Error> {
[947](https://docs.rs#947)    match text.rsplit_once(DISPLAY_SEP) {
[948](https://docs.rs#948)        None => Ok(("", text)),
[949](https://docs.rs#949)        Some((left, right)) => {
[950](https://docs.rs#950)            let right = right.trim();
[951](https://docs.rs#951)            if !right.ends_with(DISPLAY_END) {
[952](https://docs.rs#952)                Err(Error::MissingEndBracket)
[953](https://docs.rs#953)            } else {
[954](https://docs.rs#954)                let email = &right[0..right.len() - 1];
[955](https://docs.rs#955)                let display_name = left.trim();
[956](https://docs.rs#956)
[957](https://docs.rs#957)                Ok((display_name, email))
[958](https://docs.rs#958)            }
[959](https://docs.rs#959)        }
[960](https://docs.rs#960)    }

[965](https://docs.rs#965)        None => Error::MissingSeparator.into(),
[966](https://docs.rs#966)        Some(left_right) => Ok(left_right),
[967](https://docs.rs#967)    }

[970](https://docs.rs#970)fn parse_local_part(part: &str, _: Options) -> Result<(), Error> {
[971](https://docs.rs#971)    if part.is_empty() {
[972](https://docs.rs#972)        Error::LocalPartEmpty.into()
[973](https://docs.rs#973)    } else if part.len() > LOCAL_PART_MAX_LENGTH {

[975](https://docs.rs#975)    } else if part.starts_with(DQUOTE) && part.ends_with(DQUOTE) {
